title: The Rupee Has Already Hit 100 — Just Not Where You Think
excerpt: India's currency breached the psychological barrier in one-year forward markets this week, signalling that traders expect the worst of the oil shock is still ahead.
body:
The number that India's currency traders have been dreading arrived this week, but it came through the back door. While the spot rate for the Indian rupee has been grinding toward 97 against the US dollar — setting fresh record lows in almost every session since late April — the one-year forward rate quietly crossed 100. On the SGX, INR/USD futures for the May 2026 contract traded at 103.48 on Wednesday, implying that the market is already pricing in a rupee well past the century mark within twelve months.

For the millions of Indians who send money home from abroad, or for NRI families managing assets across currencies, the 100 level is not just a round number. It is a psychological threshold that rewrites the mental arithmetic of remittances, investments, and retirement planning. A rupee at 100 to the dollar means the purchasing power of dollar-denominated earnings has grown by roughly 15 per cent since the start of 2025 — good news for remitters, but a measure of just how much economic stress the currency is absorbing.

## What Is Driving the Collapse

The proximate cause is oil. Brent crude has been trading above $111 a barrel since early May, driven by the Iran conflict that erupted on February 28 and the continuing disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil, and every $10 increase in the price of a barrel adds approximately $15 billion to the annual import bill. The trade deficit has widened sharply, and foreign institutional investors have been pulling capital out of Indian equities, compounding the pressure on the currency.

DBS Group Research this week raised its USD/INR forecast to a 95-100 range for the remainder of 2026, up from 90-95 previously. Economists Radhika Rao and Philip Wee described the situation as a "stagflation-lite shock" — a combination of supply-side constraints (higher input costs, shipping delays, weaker rupee) and demand-side effects (rising pump prices, slowing fuel consumption) that leaves the Reserve Bank of India with constrained policy space.

The RBI has been intervening aggressively. State-run banks have been selling dollars on its behalf in virtually every session, and the central bank recently announced a $5 billion foreign exchange swap to shore up liquidity. But traders say the dollar supply is coming almost entirely from the RBI, not from organic market flows. "The INR is dependent on interventions," one private bank trader told Reuters. "There is constant dollar buying from clients."

## Forward Premiums Tell the Story

The forward market is where the anxiety is most visible. Offshore FX swaps reflecting India's policy rate expectations and hedging costs have widened to over 100 basis points above onshore levels, the largest gap since the 2013 taper tantrum. One-year forward premiums have dropped sharply as traders price in the possibility that the RBI may need to raise rates — or at minimum, hold them far longer than previously expected — to defend the currency.

The rupee has fallen 5.5 per cent against the dollar since the Iran conflict began, making it Asia's worst-performing currency in 2026. It has set record lows in every single month from January to May. Between sessions on some weeks, the currency hit record lows in three consecutive trading days.

## The Remittance Arithmetic

For the Indian diaspora, the rupee's slide has a paradoxical quality. Dollar-earning NRIs sending money home are getting significantly more rupees per dollar — a 20,000-rupee-per-month difference on a $2,000 monthly remittance compared to early 2025 levels. For families funding education, healthcare, or property purchases in India, the exchange rate has become a meaningful financial tailwind.

But the same forces depreciating the rupee are also eroding what those rupees can buy. Consumer price inflation in India has accelerated past 6 per cent, driven by fuel and food costs. The purchasing power gain from a favourable exchange rate is being partially eaten by higher prices on the ground. For NRIs with rupee-denominated fixed deposits, the real return after adjusting for inflation has turned negative.

## What Comes Next

The RBI's options are narrowing. Its foreign exchange reserves, while still substantial at roughly $580 billion, have declined by over $40 billion since February. Continued intervention at the current pace would further draw down reserves and risk triggering a confidence crisis of its own. Rate hikes would support the currency but slow an economy already absorbing the oil shock.

The market's message, encoded in that 103.48 forward rate, is clear: barring a resolution to the Iran conflict or a sharp drop in oil prices, the rupee breaching 100 in the spot market is not a question of if but when. For India's 32 million-strong diaspora, the century mark will be a moment to recalibrate — not just exchange rate expectations, but assumptions about the Indian economy's resilience in a world where energy shocks can still rewrite the fundamentals overnight.
